newsitem.title: USA: Senators want bipartisan commission on Medicare.
newsitem.headline: Senators want bipartisan commission on Medicare.

text.p: A leading Senate Republican said Wednesday he would push for creation of a bipartisan commission to recommend long-term changes in the Medicare health program for the elderly.

Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said he and Democratic Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, would jointly propose a new bipartisan commission on Medicare's long-term future.

Democratic aides said the legislation, which could be introduced as early as Thursday, would create a one-year commission with about 15 members. The panel would make recomendations to ensure Medicare, which serves 38 million Americans, remains solvent well into the next century.
Roth said the purpose of the panel will be "to develop a bipartisan consensus as to what needs to be done."
Moynihan of New York is the senior Democrat on the Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over Medicare, Social Security, Medicaid and other entitlements.
The support of the two senior lawmakers would increase the odds such a commision might be created.
Also Wednesday, President Clinton's proposal to cut Medicare spending by a net $138 billion over six years came under scrutiny at a House Ways and Means Committee hearing.
Lawmakers from both parties told Health Secretary Donna Shalala the plan appeared to cut federal payments to managed care providers too deeply.
The budget proposal would reduce payments to health maintenance organizations by $46 billion over six years.

Shalala told the committee the administration was not ruling out suggestions that wealthy beneficiaries pay higher premiums for Medicare Part B doctors' coverage. Clinton has said he is not opposed to such a policy, but did not include it in his budget.
The vast majority of Medicare savings in Clinton's plan come from cuts to doctors, hospitals and managed care plans.

The administration says its plan will help balance the budget and also ensure the solvency of the Medicare Part A hospital trust fund for a decade. Without policy changes, the trust fund is expected to run out of money in 2001.
But the longer-term prognosis for Medicare and other federal entitelement programs is clouded in coming years, as the wave of baby boomers begin to retire.

By the year 2030, when most baby boomers will have retired, Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security are expected to consume 17 percent of the nation's gross domestic product, about twice the current percentage. Roth noted that if the Medicare problem is not solved, it will cost $500 billion in the year 2007.
